findings.note_location: Model / How does it work? (note paragraph beginning ‘The guide describes initialization once…’)
findings.source_location: ‘Models and Construct Program Flow,’ PDF pp. 22-24, especially p. 22 lines 610-614 and p. 24 lines 644-653; ‘Intercept Function,’ p. 24.
findings.finding: The note says the cycle has Think, Update, Communicate, and Clean Up phases, omitting Intercept. The guide explicitly specifies five ordered model functions: Think, Update, Intercept, Communicate, Clean Up. Each function is completed by all models before any model advances to the next. Initialization happens once before the execution cycle. Intercept lets models modify items created by other models.
findings.required_fix: Include Intercept in the correct order and describe its cross-model message/item modification role; cite the program-flow and Intercept sections. Preserve the synchronous all-models-per-phase ordering.

findings.note_location: Model / What does it represent? and How does it work?
findings.source_location: ‘Standard Interaction Model,’ PDF pp. 50-52, especially p. 50 lines 1755-1770 and p. 51-52 lines 1817-1835.
findings.finding: The summary gives a useful framework-level account but omits defining Standard Interaction Model constraints: an agent can initiate only to agents in its directed interaction sphere; weighted partner choice incorporates physical/social/demographic proximity and knowledge similarity/expertise; activity, interaction-initiation/reception limits, and a shared communication medium constrain eligibility; interactions are formed dynamically until no initiators remain. ‘Who can find whom’ also conflates the interaction sphere with the separate realized interaction network.
findings.required_fix: Clarify the interaction-sphere versus realized interaction network terminology and either summarize the weighted selection and eligibility/update mechanics or explicitly state that this is a deliberately high-level framework summary omitting those rules. Cite the Standard Interaction Model sections/equations.

findings.source_location: ‘Simulation Period’ and ‘Generation of Agents,’ PDF pp. 4-5, lines 317-347; matching/agent assumptions and outcome models, pp. 5-9; policy definitions in Introduction pp. 2 and Methods/Virtual Experiments pp. 8-10; results Tables 1-3 and Discussion pp. 12-14.
findings.finding: The note reports the overall replication-and-policy-testing pipeline but omits defining mechanics. Agents are support seekers and volunteer counselors generated each one-minute period using empirical arrival distributions; agents receive gender, birth year, and topic characteristics drawn to match observed distributions. The status quo has counselors selecting from a live queue, seekers can cancel while waiting, and chats can be rated/blocked. The virtual experiment tests seven named policies (FCFS, LCFS, similarity using cosine similarity, gender, age, topic, and filter-based vulnerable-group policies). Waiting time, cancellations/abandonment, matching, and predicted chat outcomes depend on the model’s prediction/validation components. These rules are central to what the simulation represents and how it updates.
findings.required_fix: Expand the model description to state agent types, one-minute scheduling/arrival generation, key agent attributes, queue selection and cancellation, all tested policies, and the outcome/prediction measures; distinguish assumptions and validated replication from virtual experiments. Name further omitted mechanics explicitly and cite the source subsections/tables.
